steps.title: The build progress bar
steps.evidence: Built in S13/S15 and verified there: the bar is on Home above the fold, every pair of states differs by more than colour, each segment is labelled, and the staleness notice and derived denominator are asserted. Extended: publishing the state is a file copy onto a path no code deploy touches (/var/lib/jarvis/state), the API serves /BLOCKED.md so the why link resolves to the file rather than the dashboard, and awaiting_verification is rendered and counted apart from blocked. tests/s13b-progress-live.sh asserts all four against the live site; the console counting is asserted in tests/build-progress-summary.test.ts. PUBLISHING IS STRUCTURAL NOW, which was the actual complaint. The bar was fresh only when a human remembered to run scripts/publish-progress.sh, and that script lives on the workstation and pushes over scp - so it cannot be structural: the workstation is not always on, and nothing on the box knows it is behind. It went 21 hours stale once and was found three hours stale again today. The direction is reversed: scripts/publish-progress-pull.ts reads PROGRESS.json and BLOCKED.md straight from the repository with the admin token the box already holds, and jarvis-progress-publish.timer fires every five minutes. Nobody has to remember anything, and a stale bar now means a dead timer, which is visible, rather than a forgotten command, which is not. Validated before it is published and written by rename: a truncated PROGRESS.json served to the console would break the bar for everyone, silently, on a timer nobody watches - so a publish that does not parse fails loudly and keeps the previous good file. tests/s13b-publish-live.sh asserts all of it against the live box, and sabotaging the order so it writes before it validates leaves the console being served markdown. TIMER-PUBLISHED-CHECK.

steps.title: The retrofit sweep
steps.evidence: Five items complete (66 assertions). The step now lists nine; watchdog self-observation and Work-detail silence were added after completion. Reopened per its standing rule: done means empty right now, not closed. Item six of nine, Silence on the Work detail, is built and deployed. One correction to how the plan describes it: it says a healthy task running its test suite renders as a broken connection, and that half is already fixed - the console listens for the server's two-second heartbeat, so `live` stays true and the paused banner does not appear. What was actually missing is the useful sentence. With the stream alive and the task silent the banner read 'Live - caught up 5m ago', which is true and tells you nothing; it now reads 'running tests - 4m12s'. The quiet threshold is measured rather than chosen: gaps between events inside real heavy runs on this box cluster at 12-18 seconds with a tail at 31, 34 and 74, so a 20s cut would sit inside the ordinary distribution and flicker several times a run - the same defect in the other direction - while 30s clears it. The transport check stays first, because if the stream is gone the phase this would report cannot be trusted either. Ten assertions cover both halves (jarvis-control-center tests/live-status.test.ts); sabotaging the quiet detection so every silence reads as live failed the three working assertions. Deployed and present in the shipped work-page chunk. NOT claimed: seen rendered in a browser - there is no browser here. Item seven of nine, watchdog self-observation, is built and running. The watchdog now records each COMPLETED sweep rather than a tick - recorded after it returns, because a sweep logged on entry says the watchdog was called while one logged on exit says it finished, and only the second distinguishes a working component from one wedged on a database call. Two independent readers, because a component must not be the sole author of its own liveness: the API checks the record on its way to rendering health, and jarvis-watchdog-backstop.timer runs on the host outside docker, where it cannot be starved by whatever starved the watchdog. It takes no action - a backstop that restarts things is a second watchdog and needs a third. Coming back blind is handled too: a worker start records the gap since the last completed sweep as a blind window on the timeline, because forty unwatched minutes otherwise render as forty healthy ones, and expired leases are released on the first sweep since on this hardware one held lease in the heavy lane is the entire lane. Live: the backstop reports 'watchdog completed a sweep 7s ago (owner system-1, 3 sweeps)' from the host, and the counter is climbing. scripts/s18b-selfwatch-test.sh, 16 assertions. Sabotaged two properties and watched both go red: a component that has NEVER recorded a sweep reporting healthy (the VII.1 violation this exists to prevent - absence of data rendering as absence of problems), and lease reconciliation clearing a LIVE lease, which would take a task away from a process still working on it. NOT verified by stopping the worker in production: the incident-open path is proven against the real database by the suite instead, because the worker also drives the outbox and that is frozen. Items eight and nine done, and the register is empty. Contract conformance: both halves parse their document at run time rather than restating it, because a hand-written copy of the rules inside a test is a second thing to keep in sync and the copy is the one that rots. The taxonomy half passes - all ten implemented classes appear in ERROR_TAXONOMY.md and every retry policy matches its row. The transitions half found real drift, and measuring first is what made it useful: of 2627 transitions this system has recorded, 2576 are drawn by STATE_MACHINES.md and 51 are not, including 37 cancellations of queued tasks. A 409 guard added blind - which is what the law literally asks for - would have refused those to satisfy a document. The six shapes are in BLOCKED.md for a ruling and the suite fails on anything new. DATA_MODEL: the schema had grown to 57 tables while the file described 37; the twenty missing are now documented from the live schema, one section each, saying what the table holds AND who writes it, which is the half that is hard to recover later. scripts/s18b-datamodel-test.sh compares the document against the live schema in both directions - an undocumented table is the expected drift, a documented table that no longer exists is the one that turns the file into fiction. It immediately earned its keep twice: my first draft put three tables under one heading, which reads fine and is invisible to a per-table check, so two of them stayed undocumented while looking documented; and it found `teardown_block`, a table the fixture teardown test created and never dropped, sitting in the dev database looking exactly like an undocumented real table. The test cleans up after itself now.

steps.title: The runtime interface and a second harness
steps.evidence: Done-when observed: the same task ran to a passing pull request on BOTH harnesses, changing only tasks.runtime. Live parity run s28-parity-kws8pw, 10 passed 0 failed: claude succeeded pr=1 (13 tools), codex succeeded pr=2 (28 tools), and GitHub confirms both PRs open against the same repo, each touching src/slugify.js plus its own test. Reaching it took five runs and fixed five production defects invisible offline: IS_SANDBOX dropped by a rebase, the tripwire killing a run for reading its own auth dir, the harness never receiving the deploy key, a worktree cut from a stale origin ref, and codex overriding GIT_SSH_COMMAND with 'ssh -F /dev/null'. REPRODUCIBILITY, recorded rather than glossed: across seven live parity runs Claude reached a pull request every time it was given a working environment (four consecutive successes at the end), while Codex reached one ONCE. Its other attempts ended three different ways - push blocked by its own 'ssh -F /dev/null' overriding the supplied identity, push blocked reporting both SSH and HTTPS unavailable, and an agent.repeat loop on 'Reading additional input'. The per-run home is confirmed built each time ('key in place' in the runner log), so this is Codex's push strategy varying between runs rather than a missing key. The Done-when was observed in the world; it is not yet reliably reproducible on the second engine. CORRECTION, 2026-09-03: the reproducibility figure above blamed the engine for a defect in the prompt. The engineering loop's push phase said "push the branch", and pushing is the one thing in that loop the agent has no credential for - the deploy key belongs to Jarvis and openPullRequest uses it. Codex read the instruction, tried it, failed, and reported blocked one step from done; Claude improvised around it, so the engine that behaved correctly scored worse. With the phase changed to "stop here, Jarvis pushes", codex opened a pull request on the next run (bench-score-hides-a-failure-v0odcz/pull/1, runner log 07:01:07). "Codex reaches a PR one run in four" was never a property of Codex. Read the surviving three ways its runs ended as two, not three: the ssh -F /dev/null override and the agent.repeat loop are real and separate.

steps.title: The engineering evaluation suite
steps.evidence: The escalation half is built and asserted (scripts/s29-escalation-test.sh, 6 assertions). Rung 8 read 'switch model within the approved pool' and satisfied it with a LATERAL move - any other approved route ordered by route_order - which re-runs the same failure at the same price. It now moves only into the escalation pool, records the escalation keyed by shape so a shape that always escalates is visible without reading a log, and skips cleanly when the pool is empty. Sabotaged back to the lateral query: it grabbed an unrelated production profile that merely sorted first and recorded a phantom escalation. Every route is in the normal pool on purpose - which models are worth escalating TO is what the benchmark decides, and inventing an ordering here would be the opinion S29 exists to replace. The scorer is built and proven failable (scripts/s29-scoring-test.sh, 8 assertions): nine of the twelve dimensions are decided from evidence a run leaves behind, and root_cause_accuracy and code_quality are returned null and listed as unscored rather than invented, because a floor set from made-up components measures the invention. Weighted, not averaged - flat averaging gave a run that reproduced the bug, kept scope tight, opened a tidy PR and FIXED NOTHING a score of 0.75, which is the plan's own warning arriving in practice; it now scores 0.52 against 1.00. collectEvidence reads what a finished run recorded - phases in order, tool-call count, escalation, pull request - and is asserted against seeded rows rather than a live run, because a live run would prove the harness works and say nothing about whether the evidence was gathered correctly. Found while building it: both runtimes normalise an error event and the runner dropped them, so task_events held a run's successes and nothing else - a clean run and one that failed half its commands were indistinguishable. Fixed: migration 037 widens the runner's event vocabulary by one value and the runner persists failures, capped with the same budget as tool calls. tool_reliability is now scorable (1.00 clean, 0.50 with one failure in two calls) and still unscored when a run recorded nothing at all, because zero errors out of zero calls is an absence of evidence rather than a clean sheet. The persist path is now observed end to end: scripts/s29-error-events-test.sh drives the REAL runner with a fake stream whose tool call fails, and asserts the error row is written, carries the failing command's text, and does not replace the tool events. It also found that only Codex could report a failed tool at all - Claude reports one as a tool_result with is_error inside a user message and nothing read it, so reliability was scorable for one engine and never for the other. Both report it now. The case corpus has begun, in benchmarks/cases: each case is a seed the agent starts from and a hidden suite it never sees, so a run cannot pass by asserting its own behaviour. Two cases, both real: the slugify trailing dash (kept as the easy control that shows the harness works) and parseRange dropping the last number, taken from an Issue still open in the queue - a bug that survived a test file covering single numbers, nonsense and backwards ranges, every case except an inclusive one. scripts/s29-corpus-test.sh requires each case to FAIL against its own seed, by running it: a case whose hidden tests pass unfixed scores every engine full marks for doing nothing. The pipeline is joined and has produced real scores: scripts/s29-benchmark-run.ts seeds a case into a fresh repo, runs a real agent on it, copies the HIDDEN suite over the branch the agent produced, reverts the source to the seed to check the test it wrote actually goes red without the fix, and writes the weighted result to benchmarks. Two live rows so far, both claude on parse-range-last-number: 0.99 then 1.00 with test_quality measured. tool_reliability 0.9375 on the first is also the first live confirmation that a failed tool is recorded at all. Only root_cause_accuracy and code_quality remain unscored, and they are judgements. NOT done: the benchmark suite, the scoring, the quality floors and the measured senior_engineer route are unbuilt, and the Done-when is that route being chosen by measurement and the ranking reproducing on a re-run. THE CORPUS DISCRIMINATES: a third case, score-hides-a-failure, is taken from a bug in Jarvis itself on 2026-09-03 - the first scoreRun averaged every dimension evenly and gave a run that fixed NOTHING 0.75. Graded offline against three fixes before it was used: capping when correct is 0 scores 3 of 6 hidden tests, dropping cost scores 4 of 6, weighting and skipping unmeasured scores 6 of 6. Live, claude scored 1.00 on parse-range-last-number and 0.74 on this one, with hidden_tests 0 and correctness 1 - its own tests passed and the withheld ones failed, which is the exact scenario the seed/hidden split exists for. Its fix gated on correct and excluded cost, and still coerced null to 0, so an unmeasurable dimension scored as a failure: the third trap, predicted in the case note before the run. Still unobserved: a run scoring test_quality ZERO. FIRST TWO-ENGINE ROW: on score-hides-a-failure, claude 0.74 and codex 0.65. Both failed the hidden suite, so neither actually solved it; the gap is entirely in scope_control (1.0 against 0.5 - codex touched four files where two were expected) and pr_quality (1 against 0). CAVEAT, and it matters more than the numbers: codex scored 0 on pr_quality because it parked without opening a pull request, and its known reason for that is the environmental push problem recorded on S28 - it sets GIT_SSH_COMMAND itself and discards the identity. That is not engineering quality. As it stands the ranking conflates capability with a known environment interaction, so this pair of numbers must not be used to choose a route. Either the push problem is fixed first, or pr_quality is excluded when the run parked for an environmental reason. CONFIRMED, and it changes the reading: the benchmark row now carries the reason a run stopped, because the teardown deletes the task and a score without its reason cannot be interpreted an hour later. Codex on a second attempt scored 0.70 with scope_control 1.0, and its stored reason says in its own words that it reproduced the defect, gated on correctness, excluded cost, added regression tests, committed - and that 'Push is blocked because the environment has neither usable GitHub SSH credentials'. So BOTH engines made the same two partial fixes and both failed the hidden suite on the same third trap, null coerced to zero. On engineering they are tied on this case; the whole remaining gap between claude 0.74 and codex 0.70 is pr_quality, which is the environmental push problem and not capability. The first comparison this suite produced would have ranked two identical performances differently, which is exactly the failure mode the plan warns about. The two-engine gap is now measured rather than confounded: after the push fix codex reaches state=succeeded and scores pr_quality 1, so the earlier caveat - that the whole claude 0.74 / codex 0.70 gap was pr_quality and therefore environmental - is closed by removing the cause instead of excluding the dimension. What remains between them is scope_control (codex touched four files where two were expected) and both engines still fail the same hidden trap, which is the corpus working. Still outstanding for the Done-when: more cases drawn from bugs that took real time, quality floors set from observed scores rather than chosen, and a senior_engineer route picked by measurement and holding on a re-run. A one-case corpus where both engines tie ranks nobody. VARIANCE, measured 2026-09-03 and decisive for what is still missing: the same engine on the same case scores 0.74 and 0.67 on two runs (the second wrote no test file at all, so test_quality and red-green went unmeasured and scope_control fell to 0.5). Codex over four runs scored 0.65, 0.70, 0.70, 0.70. One engine's spread against itself, 0.07, is LARGER than the 0.04 between the two engines - so the earlier line that the remaining gap is scope_control describes one run, not a property, and nothing here ranks either engine. The Done-when therefore needs repeats per case before it needs more cases: a floor set from a single run of a single case would be set on noise, which is the failure S29 exists to prevent. Both engines still fail the same hidden trap in every one of the six runs, which is the one signal that has held steady. THIRD HARNESS ARTEFACT, and a correction: my note above that the low claude run 'wrote no test at all' was wrong. It wrote one, at src/score.test.js instead of test/score.test.js, and the red-green check looked only in test/ - so the test was never verified, test_quality was reported unmeasured, and because an unmeasured dimension is excluded WITH ITS WEIGHT, the run was scored on everything except the thing it was not credited for. Sabotaging the scorer showed the size of it: a run that adds no test scored 1.00 where a run adding a test that fails to go red scored 0.91. Writing nothing beat writing something imperfect. Fixed both ways - a test is recognised wherever the agent put it, and a run that changes code while adding no test now scores test_quality 0 rather than being excused. Separately, .jarvis/ (phases.jsonl and outcome.json, files this harness ASKS the agent to write) was counted as changed files, so two of the four codex runs lost half their scope_control for committing the bookkeeping we demanded; the reviewer already excluded that directory. Re-scoring the six stored runs with both corrected: codex mean 0.707 (n=4, spread 0.043), claude mean 0.703 (n=2, spread 0.072). The engines are indistinguishable, and the apparent claude lead was harness artefacts end to end - first the push instruction, then the bookkeeping. Noted against myself: two corrections in a row moved codex up, so the third candidate is left ALONE deliberately - claude's remaining scope_control 0.5 for putting its test beside the code is arguable, and tuning a third rule until the engines tie is the bias this step exists to prevent. Confirmed live on the corrected harness rather than by re-scoring alone: a fresh codex run at 05:44 reported files=2 where the same engine previously reported 4, scope_control 1, test_quality 1, overall 0.74 - level with the best claude run. That is the Done-when for the harness fix observed in the world. A FOURTH ARTEFACT, and it was the biggest: slug-trailing-dash shipped a CommonJS seed while the harness writes type:module, so its hidden suite died on a load error before a single test ran. The corpus check called it a good case BECAUSE it had watched it go red - failability alone cannot tell a bug from a file that will not load. Every run of that case scored hidden_tests 0 whatever the agent wrote, which is most of why 'both engines fail the same trap' looked like a finding. Cases now ship a fix/ the agent never sees and must clear both directions: red on the seed BY ASSERTION, green on the reference fix. My first discriminator for 'by assertion' counted failing tests, and node reports an unloadable file as one failing test, so the sabotage sailed through it; it now looks at what was thrown. Re-run once passable, the case separates the engines properly: claude 0.99 with the hidden suite passing, codex 0.74 with it failing - codex fell into the leading-dash trap the case was built around. THE SUITE NOW RETURNS A VERDICT. On runs not measured under a known harness defect (one rule, applied to both engines, each exclusion naming its defect): claude 0.897 over 6 runs, codex 0.783 over 4, three cases each, margin 0.115 against the 0.072 noise band. Separating dimension is hidden_tests, 0.67 to 0.25. Derived floor 0.67, the winner's worst run. src/ranking.ts refuses rather than guesses - too few runs, too few cases, or a gap inside the noise band all return a reason instead of a number, and a tie yields no floor at all. What is NOT yet true, stated plainly: routing already ordered claude ahead of codex (route_order 5 against 15) by opinion, so the measurement CONFIRMS that order rather than having chosen it. The Done-when needs route_order written from the ranking, and a second independent pass reproducing it. MORE CASES MADE THEM LOOK MORE ALIKE, NOT LESS. The plan's Debug note for an undecided suite is to add cases from bugs that took real time, so two were added from tonight's own production bugs: red-for-the-wrong-reason (a hidden suite that could not load was counted as a case failing honestly) and notify-about-its-own-channel (the notice telling you to pair WhatsApp, queued on WhatsApp). Both are gradeable in both directions against a reference fix. Live on both engines they TIED: red-for-the-wrong-reason 0.74 to 0.74 with neither solving the hidden suite, and notify-about-its-own-channel 1.00 to 0.96 with both solving it. Pooled over 22 valid runs across 5 cases the ranking is claude by 0.083, down from 0.115 on three cases; the second pass is claude by 0.055, INSIDE the 0.072 band, so scripts/s29-reproduce.ts still reports NOT REPRODUCED. Adding cases narrowed the gap rather than widening it, which is itself the measurement: on this kind of work the two engines are close enough that the suite declines to order them, and the honest reading is that a senior_engineer choice between these two cannot yet be made on quality. red-for-the-wrong-reason earned its place immediately by catching a defect in the checker that grades it - the gradeability check matched the load-error words appearing in the case's own test data before checking for an assertion, which is precisely the bug the case describes. Also fixed, found through a leaked fixture: teardown met the cycle tasks -> issues -> tasks (an issue belongs to a task, a task can be blocked BY an issue), stopped at a fixed depth and returned silently - which did not stop the deletes above it, so tasks went while their issues stayed and the whole thing rolled back. Four benchmark projects leaked that way, and a rolled-back teardown reports 'cleaned up' with an empty list, which reads like success. The nullable link that closes the cycle is now set to NULL, an unbreakable cycle throws rather than half-deleting, and scripts/s29-teardown-cycle-test.sh builds the cycle on purpose. Verified against the real leaked projects: all three cleared with leftBehind empty. THE SUITE WAS FED A DELIBERATELY BAD RUN, which the plan asks for and nothing had done: scripts/s29-fluent-fraud.sh scripts a run that announces every phase, touches exactly the expected files, adds a test, keeps the suite green, opens a pull request and claims success with high confidence - and fixes nothing, its test asserting the behaviour the code already has. It is scored through the SAME measuring path as a real run (measureBranch, now shared, so a second copy cannot let the suite pass frauds while the fraud check reports all is well). It scored 0.652 against a floor of 0.67: it cleared by 0.014, which is not a suite catching a fraud, it is a suite missing one by luck. Two defects behind that. FIRST, a double count: regressionTestsPassed and ownTestsPassed were fed the SAME boolean, so one self-certified fact - the tests I wrote pass - carried 4 of the 11.5 weight. No case in this corpus seeds tests of its own, so not breaking them was never an achievement; it is null now, and the fraud fell to 0.579. SECOND, and larger: the floor was the winner's worst run of ANY kind. The scores are cleanly bimodal - every run that passed the withheld suite scored 0.96 to 1.00, every run that failed it scored 0.67 to 0.74, and nothing has ever landed between - so the winner's worst run is a run that did not solve the problem, and a floor derived from it sat 0.009 above a scripted fraud. A floor that admits work indistinguishable from fluent fraud is not a floor. It is now derived from runs that passed the tests they never saw, and refuses when the winner has none: 0.99, with the fraud 0.411 clear below it. Sabotaged the derivation to ignore solving and watched it hand back 0.73 from runs that solved nothing. The bimodality is the most useful thing measured tonight: on this corpus a run either solves the case or it does not, and the middle of the range is empty, so a floor belongs in the gap rather than at the bottom of the losing cluster. THE MEAN WAS THE WRONG STATISTIC, and the two methods disagree on the only decision that matters. Because the scores are bimodal, an average tracks the MIX of solved and unsolved runs rather than either cluster - it turns 'how OFTEN this engine succeeds' into a decimal that invites comparison against a threshold. Ranking by solve rate instead (did the run pass the withheld suite): claude 7/12 = 58 percent, codex 3/10 = 30 percent. A 28-point gap, which sounds decisive and is not: at these sample sizes it is 1.39 standard errors, inside sampling noise. By mean the same runs gave claude a win by 0.083 against an eyeballed 0.072 band, so the earlier ranking was calling noise a result - the band was a heuristic, the standard error is computed. The suite now refuses and says what would settle it: about 23 runs per engine, so 11 more for claude and 13 for codex. That turns 'needs more data' from a shrug into a number. scripts/s29-apply-route.ts is wired to the solve rate, so the route derivation now refuses too and changes nothing, which is the truthful state; the audit trail already carries the correction that the earlier ranking did not reproduce. Sabotaged the significance test and watched it call a 28-point gap a win and order two engines with identical rates over thirty runs each. THE CAMPAIGN RAN AND THE ANSWER IS STILL NO, for a reason worth keeping. Twenty runs, two full passes over all five cases on both engines. The estimate is remarkably stable - claude solves 63-64 percent in every window measured and codex 33-40 - and the two passes returned IDENTICAL rates, 3/5 against 2/5, twice. But the significance depends entirely on which runs are pooled: everything ever recorded (45 runs) gives claude at 2.04 sigma, the runs made since the corpus reached five cases (27) give 1.39, and the campaign alone (21) gives 1.11. Only the widest window clears the bar, and it clears it by mixing runs made against a three-case corpus - including codex runs made while harness defects since fixed were costing it points. Reporting 2.04 would mean widening the window until the number was the one I wanted, which is precisely the failure this step exists to prevent, so the claim is not made. The suite says what it needs: about 28-34 runs per engine on the current corpus, against 11 and 10 today, so roughly three more full passes. Two corrections landed while checking. rankingReproduces demanded that EACH pass independently reach significance, which the plan does not ask and which five cases cannot supply - a pass is five runs per engine, so it refused two identical results for want of power, a check measuring its own sample size. It now asks the plan's actual question: is there a ranking on everything pooled, and do the passes agree without wild variance - with the pooled significance requirement untouched, because that is the half that must never be relaxed. And it reproduced by MEAN rather than solve rate, which would only have proven the wrong statistic is consistent. Also verified live this tick: the worktree fetch fix is deployed and a real heavy run now logs zero 'fetch of origin/main failed' warnings, where every run for weeks logged one.

steps.title: Memory and knowledge
steps.evidence: Started with the piece the plan says decides whether any of it works: "retrieval quality is mostly a chunking problem, and uniform chunking is the commonest cause of bad answers". src/chunk.ts branches on content - prose on the headings the author already chose, chat on a message plus the two around it because 'yes, do that' is unanswerable alone, transcripts on whole speaker turns because a turn split mid-sentence loses who said it, code on symbols because half a function retrieves as neither, tables repeating the header row on every window because rows without it mean nothing, and short notes not at all. Two rules hold everywhere: a call chunks ONE document, enforced by the signature so there is no way to hand it two, and every chunk carries a locator and a character offset so a citation can say 'function total' rather than 'somewhere in this file' and a wrong answer is traceable to the chunk that caused it. scripts/s30-chunk-test.sh, 15 assertions, each one a way a fixed window produces a fluent wrong answer. Sabotaged by replacing the branching with a single 1200-character window - the exact thing the plan warns about - and it failed five assertions across four content types, including a chunk spanning two headings and two functions landing in one chunk. ADR 019 records the architecture decision and, more usefully, what would overturn it: a measured miss rate on real questions where the right chunk exists and lexical ranking does not surface it. It does NOT claim lexical search matches semantic search on paraphrase - that is a real limitation, stated. Migration 039 gives knowledge_chunks the tsvector (generated, so it cannot drift from the body), a GIN index, and kind/locator/char_offset/chunk_index/source_date - the date stored now although nothing reads it, because S41 needs a time index and backfilling a date nobody recorded is guesswork. NOT built yet: ingestion, the four tiers, ranking, citation, and the superseded-version problem where a replaced document answers fluently from the version that was replaced. Ingestion and ranked retrieval follow. src/knowledge.ts keeps both halves together on purpose - ingestion writes what a citation will need and retrieval hands it back, and splitting them across files is how a writer stops storing a field the reader still expects. Ranked with ts_rank_cd rather than ts_rank: cover density rewards a chunk where the query terms sit near each other, which is what 'the passage that actually discusses this' looks like. Three rules the plan is specific about are now enforced and asserted. TIERS ARE NEVER MERGED - a chunk of a PDF returned when the honest answer is 'you decided that on the 14th, here is the task' is a wrong answer that looks right, so the caller gets the tiers apart, each hit labelled, and activity first because a decision has a date and a task and can be cited most precisely. A SUPERSEDED DOCUMENT DOES NOT ANSWER - v2 replaces v1 and both are kept, their chunks indistinguishable in the index, so without the filter 'what did the client say about the refund window?' is answered fluently, with a citation, from the version that was replaced; it stays reachable when history is asked for deliberately. AND RE-INGESTING REPLACES rather than leaving two generations competing, which reads as the document saying two things. scripts/s30-retrieval-test.sh, 14 assertions against a real database. Sabotaged twice at once - letting the replaced version answer, and merging the tiers into one sorted list - and six assertions went red including the project-scope leak. Two bugs found by running it: a parameter Postgres refuses because the query never mentions it (there is no context to infer a type from), and a test fixture short enough to fall under the leave-it-whole threshold, so it was exercising the wrong branch. NOT built yet: the four tiers as a queryable API surface, the console, and ingestion wired to what actually arrives. Scenario N2 is now most of the way there. A forwarded thread was being STORED but not indexed - S37 keeps a forward separately so it can never be mistaken for something he said, and that is right, but stored is not the same as kept: a thread nobody can retrieve has been filed, and nobody discovers that until the day they ask. Forwards are chunked as chat on arrival now, so the message that answers a question three weeks later comes back with the two around it and a citation naming the forward. And the second half of the Done-when is built rather than assumed: an honest 'I do not know'. The natural shape of this system is the opposite - retrieval returns the three least-irrelevant chunks and a model writes a confident paragraph from them, and nothing in that path ever says 'there was nothing here'. So the decision is made on whether anything was retrieved at all, before any prose exists, and the refusal names every tier it looked in so the no is checkable. scripts/s30-dump-test.sh, 10 assertions; sabotaging it to answer with nothing and to file without indexing failed five, including the cross-project leak. Two of my own mistakes worth recording: I passed a parameter the statement never mentions - the identical bug I had fixed an hour earlier in the same file and written a comment about - and the first version named the forward by updating rows written in the last minute, which is a race dressed as a query, since two forwards arriving together would relabel each other. The name is written with the chunk now. NOT done: PDFs need text extraction, which does not exist yet, so N2 is proven on the thread and not on the three documents; and the Done-when also asks for this to survive a restore from backup. Text extraction closes the PDF half of N2. src/extract.ts reads PDFs, text, markdown, CSV, JSON, source and HTML, and picks the chunking kind from the mime type first and the extension second - a mime type is what the sender claimed and an extension is what the file is called, and the first is usually the better guess. HTML is stripped of scripts and styles before indexing, or a page retrieves on the word 'function'. The rule that matters more than the format list: extraction returns a REASON when it fails and never an empty string, because a document that extracts to nothing is stored, indexed and permanently unanswerable while looking exactly like a document with nothing to say. That guard immediately caught a real defect in the library: pdf-parse v2 separates pages with lines like '-- 1 of 3 --', so a scanned image-only PDF extracts to a NON-empty string containing only page markers, sails past an emptiness check, and is stored as a successful ingest of a document that can never answer anything. Markers are stripped before the emptiness decision now. There is a size ceiling, because extraction runs in the same process as everything else and a 400 MB log would take the worker down - refusing is honest, dying is not. scripts/s30-extract-test.sh builds a genuinely valid PDF by hand rather than committing a fixture, so the test exercises a real parse; using the same library to write and read would only prove it agrees with itself. 10 assertions; sabotaged to return empty success on unsupported formats and to count page markers as content, and both went red. Also worth recording: pdf-parse v2 is a class with getText(), not the v1 default-exported function every example still shows. Uploaded documents are indexed on arrival now, so 'all stored, chunked, indexed' is true of the PDFs and not only of the thread. Two gates run before any text is read, and the first is a security property rather than a nicety: A QUARANTINED ARTIFACT IS NEVER INDEXED. S17 refuses to serve one to a model or a browser, and indexing it would carry its contents into an answer by another door - with a citation, looking entirely legitimate. A quarantine gate that guards the front door and not the index is not a quarantine gate, and the suite asserts the leak directly rather than trusting the refusal: with the gate open, blocked text comes back in a retrieval result. The second gate is that an unreadable document is REPORTED rather than skipped - it lands on the activity timeline naming the file, because a line in a container log is not visible to anyone, and a file that was stored and never mentioned is indistinguishable from one that indexed cleanly and had nothing to say. The difference only surfaces on the day he asks it a question. Indexing is also not allowed to throw into the upload path: losing the file is worse than losing its searchability, so a failure to index still stores the artifact and says so. scripts/s30-index-artifact-test.sh, 8 assertions; sabotaging the gate and the reporting failed four, including the leak. S17's own 75 assertions still pass, so the artifact path is undisturbed. Asking is now reachable and deployed. /api/ask is deliberately a different route from /api/search rather than a flag on it: search finds things by substring and orders them by recency, which is right for 'where is that task' and wrong for 'what did the client say about the refund window'. The new one ranks by relevance, keeps the tiers separate all the way to the caller - flattening them one layer from the screen would undo the whole point - and returns known:false with a reason, so a caller CANNOT accidentally render a confident answer because there is nothing to render. Verified against the live box rather than in dev: tests/s30-ask-live.sh checks that migration 039 actually applied there (all five retrieval columns, and the GIN index, so ranking is not a sequential scan), that the route is registered and refuses an anonymous caller with 401, and that a seeded document comes back with a citation while an unanswerable question comes back as an honest no. 6 assertions. Seen to fail: the route was renamed, deployed, and the live check reported 'the route is not registered (404) - the deploy did not carry it', then restored and redeployed. Every layer between the query and the answer - Caddy, the API container, the session, the migration - has failed at least once in this project while every unit test stayed green, which is why this one is live. Which tier answers is now decided by the QUESTION rather than by a fixed preference, which is what the plan actually asks: prefer whichever answer can be cited most precisely. A why- or when-did-we-decide question leads with activity, because a decision has a date and an actor; a what-did-they-say question leads with the document, because a document can be quoted. Memory is last in both orders always - it is the only tier whose contents nobody can check, and putting it above evidence that can be quoted is how a half-remembered instruction outranks the contract it contradicts. A small keyword rule rather than a model call, because this decides ORDERING and not truth: every tier is still returned and labelled. Config changes now answer too, which the plan names explicitly - a decision lives in activity_events AND config_versions, and the config row is the better-evidenced half because it carries the value, the actor, the note and the message that caused it. Keys are searched with underscores turned into spaces, or 'why is the deploy policy manual' never reaches deploy_policy. scripts/s30-which-tier-test.sh, 10 assertions; sabotaging the ordering back to static and dropping config decisions failed seven. THE BUG THAT COST THIS TICK, and it is the worst instance of a trap already in DEBUG_NOTES: python writes backslash-b as an actual BACKSPACE character, so the decision regexes shipped as /<BS>why did<BS>/i - eleven patterns containing invisible control characters. They survived grep, survived tsc, compiled, and matched nothing. Found by printing charCodeAt on the regex source: 8,119,104,121... The fix is to build backslashes with chr(92) and to read the result through cat -v, which renders them as ^H. Two of my own test assertions were also wrong and both in the same way: websearch_to_tsquery ANDs its terms, so a question containing a word that appears nowhere matches nothing, and I twice demanded a hit that should not exist. Corrected a deviation from the plan that I had introduced: a superseded document was being silently DROPPED, and the plan asks for both halves - the current version answers, and the replaced one is offered AS superseded. Dropping it means nobody can see what changed; ranking it means the answer is confidently out of date. Superseded chunks now come back last, labelled in the citation where a reader will actually see it, and the includeSuperseded flag is gone because it had become a filter expression that was always true - a line that reads like a filter and filters nothing is worse than no line. The test caught a second, subtler fault in itself: with two short documents the assertion 'the current version answers first' passed on relevance alone, so sabotaging the ordering left it green. The fixture now makes the SUPERSEDED document the richer one, so it outranks its own replacement and only the explicit ordering can put the current version first - and with that, removing the ordering fails the assertion with 'the first hit was contracts/acme-v1.md (superseded)'. The plan's own end-to-end test now runs: one document of each type, each asked a question only answerable from its MIDDLE - which is the point, because a question answerable from the first paragraph passes even when chunking is broken. A PDF (a name twenty sections in), a chat export (a line about invoicing among forty), a call transcript (one turn, still carrying its speaker), a source file (a function halfway down, with its body), a spreadsheet (a row forty below its header, returned WITH the header), and a three-word note that comes back whole. 18 assertions. IT FOUND A REAL CHUNKER DEFECT, and exactly the one the plan's Debug section warns about: prose with no blank lines was never split, so a 17,933-character document became ONE chunk however long it was - 'a whole 40-page document as one chunk will defeat any ranker'. Most text extracted from a PDF has no blank lines, so this was the common case rather than an edge. A paragraph that is itself enormous is now split on line boundaries: the same document becomes 16 chunks and the sentence at its very end is retrievable again. Sabotaged back to a single chunk and watched it fail. One fixture limitation stated rather than hidden: the hand-written PDF generator emits a single page, so lines past about the fiftieth sit at a negative y coordinate and are not extracted - a 400-line PDF was testing my generator rather than the ingest path. The size property is asserted on a long text document instead, and a PDF that fits its page is asserted answerable to its last line.
